challenges.title: A/B test z-test
challenges.prompt: Implement two_proportion_z(conv_a, n_a, conv_b, n_b) using the pooled-proportion z-test and a two-sided p-value from the normal CDF (math.erf). Analyze 200/2000 vs 250/2000 and then a small 200/2000 vs 210/2000 difference.
challenges.starter:
import math

def two_proportion_z(conv_a, n_a, conv_b, n_b):
    # return (p_a, p_b, z, two_sided_p) using the pooled-proportion z-test;
    # p-value from the normal CDF: 0.5*(1+erf(z/sqrt(2)))
    return 0, 0, 0, 1

p_a, p_b, z, p = two_proportion_z(200, 2000, 250, 2000)
print("A=%.3f B=%.3f lift=%.1f%%" % (p_a, p_b, (p_b - p_a) / p_a * 100))
print("z=%.2f p=%.4f" % (z, p))
print("significant at 5%:", p < 0.05)
_, _, z2, p2 = two_proportion_z(200, 2000, 210, 2000)
print("small difference p=%.2f significant: %s" % (p2, p2 < 0.05))
challenges.expected:
A=0.100 B=0.125 lift=25.0%
z=2.50 p=0.0124
significant at 5%: True
small difference p=0.60 significant: False
challenges.solution:
import math

def two_proportion_z(conv_a, n_a, conv_b, n_b):
    p_a, p_b = conv_a / n_a, conv_b / n_b
    pooled = (conv_a + conv_b) / (n_a + n_b)
    se = math.sqrt(pooled * (1 - pooled) * (1 / n_a + 1 / n_b))
    z = (p_b - p_a) / se
    p_value = 2 * (1 - 0.5 * (1 + math.erf(abs(z) / math.sqrt(2))))
    return p_a, p_b, z, p_value

p_a, p_b, z, p = two_proportion_z(200, 2000, 250, 2000)
print("A=%.3f B=%.3f lift=%.1f%%" % (p_a, p_b, (p_b - p_a) / p_a * 100))
print("z=%.2f p=%.4f" % (z, p))
print("significant at 5%:", p < 0.05)
_, _, z2, p2 = two_proportion_z(200, 2000, 210, 2000)
print("small difference p=%.2f significant: %s" % (p2, p2 < 0.05))
challenges.explain: A 2.5-point lift on 2,000 users per arm is unlikely under no difference, while a 0.5-point lift isn't distinguishable from noise. Report effect size and interval too. Verified by running the solution.

challenges.title: Least squares and a warning
challenges.prompt: Implement fit_line(x, y) returning slope, intercept and R-squared by ordinary least squares. Fit a clean linear dataset, predict x=7, and then fit data with one outlier to see how it distorts the line.
challenges.starter:
def fit_line(x, y):
    # ordinary least squares: return (slope, intercept, r_squared)
    return 0, 0, 0

x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
y = [2.1, 4.3, 5.9, 8.2, 9.9, 12.1]
m, c, r2 = fit_line(x, y)
print("slope=%.3f intercept=%.3f r2=%.4f" % (m, c, r2))
print("prediction for x=7: %.2f" % (c + m * 7))

# Anscombe-style warning: same fit, different shape
x2 = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
y2 = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 30]
m2, c2, r22 = fit_line(x2, y2)
print("outlier fit slope=%.2f r2=%.2f" % (m2, r22))
challenges.expected:
slope=1.974 intercept=0.173 r2=0.9983
prediction for x=7: 13.99
outlier fit slope=4.57 r2=0.70
challenges.solution:
def fit_line(x, y):
    n = len(x)
    mx, my = sum(x) / n, sum(y) / n
    sxx = sum((a - mx) ** 2 for a in x)
    sxy = sum((a - mx) * (b - my) for a, b in zip(x, y))
    slope = sxy / sxx
    intercept = my - slope * mx
    ss_res = sum((b - (intercept + slope * a)) ** 2 for a, b in zip(x, y))
    ss_tot = sum((b - my) ** 2 for b in y)
    return slope, intercept, 1 - ss_res / ss_tot

x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
y = [2.1, 4.3, 5.9, 8.2, 9.9, 12.1]
m, c, r2 = fit_line(x, y)
print("slope=%.3f intercept=%.3f r2=%.4f" % (m, c, r2))
print("prediction for x=7: %.2f" % (c + m * 7))

# Anscombe-style warning: same fit, different shape
x2 = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
y2 = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 30]
m2, c2, r22 = fit_line(x2, y2)
print("outlier fit slope=%.2f r2=%.2f" % (m2, r22))
challenges.explain: The first fit is nearly perfect, while one outlier at x=6 changes the slope sharply and drops R-squared. Always plot your data and inspect residuals. Verified by running the solution.
